summary: All 15 saved English paragraphs and all seven lesson objects were reviewed against the bound Chinese edition and raw transcription. The principal scientific safeguards are retained, but 'within each grain' overstates grain-level participation in slip. Undefined prerequisite terms and compressed causal steps also prevent acceptance for a strong eight-year-old self-reader. Four focused findings require revision; no author, product, figure, or native artifact was changed.

source.scope: English textual coverage and fidelity to the bound transcribed source and Chinese comparator, not original scan or Chinese science approval
source.reason: The five source prose blocks, figure slot, and caption retain their order, source references, and main claims. Elastic displacement, accumulated plastic displacement, retained crystalline order with qualifications, the two-panel slip explanation, local initiation, and the polycrystal comparison are all represented. Definitions added in English do not remove a source claim. Scientific acceptance of an inherited generalization is assessed separately under science.

science.reason: Flow paragraph 11 says slip occurs 'within each grain'. Slip-dominated plastic deformation of a polycrystal does not require every grain to undergo slip, especially when plastic deformation is first beginning. Some grains can remain elastic while others slip. This is a substantive quantifier correction even though similar wording occurs in the Chinese comparator.

simultaneousRigidPlaneDisplacement.reason: The text explicitly identifies panel b as a model of the result and denies that complete atomic layers must move simultaneously as rigid units. Local, gradual dislocation motion and local initiation are stated.

universalMaterialApplicability.reason: The proposed mechanism is consistently discussed in crystals and under slip-dominated conditions. The text does not assert that it explains all noncrystalline materials. It expressly rejects an unconditional ranking of any polycrystal against any single-crystal orientation. F01 concerns all grains participating, a distinct overstatement that these bulk-material caveats do not repair.

elasticRecoveryNotMicroscopicImmobility.reason: Atoms shift during elastic deformation; recovery after unloading is approximate and conditional on no damage or irreversible process. The text does not say that atoms are motionless. Readability repairs must preserve this distinction and describe recovery of average positions rather than freezing microscopic motion.

crystallineOrderNotUnchangedNeighborsOrP.reason: Retained order is limited to the relevant slip conditions; unchanged neighbors and a defect-free lattice are expressly disclaimed.

defectsNotAlwaysSoftening.reason: The text distinguishes structures that help slip from those that obstruct dislocation motion rather than making all defects universal weak spots.

figureContextApplicability.reason: The English context retains the source/Chinese roles: panel a is associated with slip marks on a stretched single crystal, and panel b with a simplified relative offset of lattice layers. It bounds the latter as a representation of the slip result, not simultaneous rigid movement. No new visual content is required by these roles. F03 requires clearer English explanations around the existing figure, not a figure replacement.
figureContextApplicability.actualAssetUnchanged: reported by the bound inventory only; not independently checked in this assignment

readability.targetReader: strong eight-year-old self-reader without an adult translating terminology
readability.reason: The opening introduces chemical elements, elastic range, strains, crystal, equilibrium positions, load, and irreversible process without enough local explanation. The slip mechanism then relies on planes, tension, stress, shear, and line defect. The final comparison assumes orientation, grain boundaries, accommodation, and fine-grained material. A lattice definition and a polycrystal definition are useful, but do not supply these missing links.

flow.reason: The saved flow contains the draft's prose paragraphs in the same order, and the two boundaries fit the transitions to lattice slip and polycrystals. There is no missing English paragraph or misplaced source object. However, prerequisite ideas are used before they are explained, and the reader is taken from named mechanisms directly into qualifications without a concrete causal bridge. The three small definition/causal repairs should occur at the existing first-use locations; a whole-lesson reorder is unnecessary.

bindings.criticalHashVerification: Each of the six input files was read and hashed once before freezing; the actual English draft, not merely the author manifest, was bound.

findings.title: Not every grain must slip
findings.exactText: When plastic deformation occurs mainly through slip, slip also occurs within each grain.
findings.finding: The universal 'each grain' is stronger than the correct grain-level mechanism. A polycrystal can accumulate plastic strain through slip in some grains while other grains remain elastic; differently oriented grains do not all have to start slipping together. The later caveat about comparing any polycrystal with any single crystal does not qualify this assertion.
findings.comparison: The Chinese comparator likewise uses an all-grains formulation; its status or historical reports are not science approval. The raw source discusses slip in individual small crystals, which can be explained without requiring universal participation.

smallestRepair.suggestedText: When plastic deformation occurs mainly through slip, slip can occur inside individual grains. It need not begin in all grains at once.
smallestRepair.preserve: The following explanation that grain orientations and easy-slip planes/directions differ, and the qualified bulk-material comparison.

findings.title: The opening assumes the vocabulary it needs to teach
exactText: Atoms are the basic units of chemical elements.
Within the elastic range of small strains, the atoms in a crystal shift slightly from their original equilibrium positions.
After the load is removed, the atoms can return approximately to their original positions if no damage or other irreversible process has occurred.
findings.finding: Explaining atoms through 'chemical elements' substitutes another unknown term. Crystal, deformation, elastic range, strain, equilibrium position, and load then arrive before their meanings or an observable push/pull example. The permanent-change contrast in paragraph 1 is useful, but the reader still cannot independently translate the opening into what changes, what is removed, and what returns. The scientific recovery conditions should not be discarded to solve this.

smallestRepair.operation: rewrite the opening and explain the unloading sentence in the same prose block; retain its two-step change/recovery sequence
guidance: Give atoms a plain-language particle explanation and a crystal its repeating arrangement at first use.
Explain deformation as a change in shape; use a small push or pull before naming load or strain.
Explain elastic as recovering the original shape after the push/pull is removed, and plastic as leaving a permanent change.
Describe equilibrium positions as average positions around which the atoms move, not microscopic immobility.
Retain approximate recovery and the absence of damage or other irreversible change; explain irreversible as a change that does not undo when the push/pull stops.
smallestRepair.suggestedLocalPhrase: A load is a push or pull. When it changes a crystal's shape only a little, the atoms shift a little from their usual average positions.
smallestRepair.notRequested: A separate glossary, a new example figure, or a new lesson section.

findings.title: Slip and dislocation motion need a concrete causal bridge
exactText: Slip is the relative movement of parts of a crystal along particular planes.
The stress produced by tension has a shearing effect along suitable crystal planes and directions, helping slip occur.
A dislocation is a line defect in the ordered arrangement of a crystal.
findings.finding: The slip definition uses an unexplained plane, the lattice definition comes only afterward, and the Figure 91 introduction assumes single crystal, tension, stress, and shear. Naming a dislocation as a 'line defect' does not tell this reader what is imperfect or how its local movement permits a lasting shift. Paragraphs 8-10 consequently rely on a mechanism whose name has been supplied but whose causal step has not. The correct anti-rigid-plane caveat in paragraph 6 should remain.

smallestRepair.operation: expand the existing first-use definitions and replace the compressed shear/dislocation sentences; do not move the figure or redesign the lesson
guidance: Explain a crystal plane as a flat layer in the repeating arrangement when defining slip.
Explain single crystal as one crystal rather than many small crystals joined, and tension as a pull.
Explain stress as force per unit area, then shear as the tendency of neighboring parts to slide past one another.
Turn 'line defect' into a line where the repeating arrangement does not fit perfectly; add the small local rearrangement step.
smallestRepair.suggestedDislocationText: A dislocation is a line where the crystal's repeating arrangement does not fit perfectly. As this defect moves, nearby particles rearrange in small steps, allowing one part of the crystal to shift past another.
smallestRepair.suggestedModelClarification: The model shows the offset left after slip; it does not show an entire atomic layer moving all at once.
smallestRepair.preserve: The panel a/panel b context, the simplified-result limitation, and the statement that real slip often proceeds locally rather than as simultaneous rigid movement.

findings.title: The grain comparison lacks plain referents and a worked causal link
exactText: Different grains usually have different orientations, so the planes and directions along which slip occurs most easily also differ.
Neighboring grains must accommodate one another's deformation, and grain boundaries can obstruct slip.
The textbook notes that this effect is more noticeable in fine-grained materials.
This comparison applies to the relevant materials and slip conditions.
Material composition, orientations produced by processing, temperature, and loading conditions all affect the result.
findings.finding: The polycrystal/grain definition is helpful, but orientation, grain boundary, accommodate, and fine-grained are not explained. 'This effect' refers to the greater starting stress but requires the child to reconstruct that link, and 'relevant materials and slip conditions' supplies no usable referent. The final abstract list of factors is correct in purpose but still needs translation into what the material is made of, which way its patterns face, and how it is pushed or pulled.

smallestRepair.operation: add short first-use glosses and one fitting/slip causal sentence inside the existing final prose block; keep the qualified comparison
guidance: Explain orientation as which way a grain's repeating pattern faces.
Explain grain boundary as the place where two grains meet and fine-grained as made of smaller grains.
Explain accommodation as neighboring grains still needing to fit against one another while they change shape.
Name the effect explicitly as extra stress needed to start permanent deformation.
Make clear that the comparison concerns the same material under comparable temperature/loading and suitable slip conditions; retain the exception for single-crystal orientation.
Replace the closing abstract list with plain equivalents rather than deleting its limitations.
smallestRepair.suggestedCausalText: A grain boundary is where two grains meet. As a grain changes shape, it must still fit against its neighbors. The boundary can hinder slip, so more stress may be needed before permanent deformation starts.
smallestRepair.suggestedClosingText: What the material is made of, which way its grain patterns face after processing, its temperature, and how it is pushed or pulled also affect the result.
smallestRepair.preserve: No universal polycrystal/single-crystal ranking, no claim of completely random orientations, and no judgment based on grain size alone.

coverage.titleChapterAndPrintedTitle: The mechanism title, Chapter 6 heading, and printed title retain the source subject and number. The generic title is narrowed by the prose's repeated crystal/slip scope.

paragraphs.assessment: Small elastic displacements are retained; opening terminology is not self-readable.
Approximate conditional recovery and permanent-change contrast are retained; load and irreversible process need plain equivalents.
Accumulated displacement can exceed initial particle spacing; unloading leaves deformation. No universal numerical threshold is asserted.
Slip-dominated, no-fracture/no-transformation scope is retained; plane and relative movement need concrete explanation.
Lattice has a useful repeating-pattern definition; unchanged neighbors and defect-free order are correctly rejected. Relate defects to an imperfection before later dislocation use.
Panel a and shear-driven slip retain the Chinese/source context; tension, stress, shear, and single crystal need first-use bridges.
Panel b is correctly limited to a simplified result and denies necessary rigid simultaneous movement. The retained Latin-label statement is textual, not an observed asset claim.
Local gradual dislocation motion is stated but line defect requires a concrete arrangement-and-motion explanation.
Local initiation and the source's irregular-atom-group illustration are retained; not all-volume simultaneous slip.
The text properly rejects a universal weak-atom-group starting mechanism; depends on the earlier dislocation explanation repaired by F03.
Helping and obstructing effects are distinguished correctly; depends on the earlier defect/motion bridge repaired by F03.
Polycrystal/grain definition is supplied, but each-grain participation is overclaimed and orientation needs a plain referent.
Qualified greater starting stress is retained, but accommodation, grain boundaries, fine grains, and 'this effect' need a causal/lexical bridge.
Universal ranking is expressly rejected, but 'relevant materials and slip conditions' is too vague for an independent comparison.
Orientation need not be random; composition, processing, temperature, and loading qualifications remain. Plain equivalents are needed.

Caption text is translated and remains attached to the same figure. Chinese label metadata is retained; runtime exposure was not inspected.

flowBoundaries.assessment: Correct transition from elastic/plastic behavior and retained order to the lattice-slip explanation.
Correct transition from local slip/defects to polycrystals and grain interactions.
